title: Currencies: Short bets on Aussie dollar surge to record
full_text:
A high-stakes clash is brewing over the outlook for the Australian dollar as fund managers build the biggest bet against the currency on record over souring artificial intelligence sentiment, locking horns with hedge funds that still expect the currency to rally.
Weekly data from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) showed asset managers held a record short position in the Australian dollar, worth $12.9 billion as of October 20. The massive bet, which makes money if the Aussie falls, highlights the new relationship between the risk-sensitive currency and sentiment around the tech sector.
"The Aussie is increasingly becoming an AI trade," said Oliver Levingston, a Bank of America foreign exchange strategist. "The Aussie moves as such a high beta to risk assets, so it makes sense for Aussie shorts to be accumulating as a hedge against an equity market sell-off."
He added that one of the bull cases for the Australian dollar was the massive level of capital expenditure in data centres that would drive economic growth and support the currency.
"We assume that the $180 billion pipeline of data centres will roll out, but if sentiment around AI worsens, it will threaten the pipeline," he warned. Wall Street has come under pressure recently from a resurgence in the oil price, surging bond yields and a sell-off in the tech sector as confidence in the AI trade comes under threat. Anthropic's highly anticipated blockbuster IPO next month will be the next litmus test for investors.
Australia's $4.8 trillion superannuation funds, which are heavily exposed to Wall Street, are building short positions in the Australian dollar to offset some of the loss from a global rout in equities. "As a super fund asset manager, you want that downside risk protection," said Levingston. "It makes perfect sense."
With equity markets starting to show cracks, credit risk climbing and the Reserve Bank of Australia closer to the peak of its interest-rate cycle than other central banks, the Bank of America strategist said the pressure points were building in the currency.
Compounding investor fears around the Australian dollar - often viewed as proxy for global growth - is a darkening economic outlook.
Sean Callow, a foreign exchange analyst at InTouch Capital Markets, said it was particularly concerning that the short positions building in the currency were from "real money" accounts like institutional investors.
"They're the ones taking the longer-term view and it gives the impression that there is considerable pessimism over the global economy heading into 2027," he said. "This will have a flow-on impact to a very trade-sensitive country like Australia. The positioning of these accounts suggests that the Aussie dollar will be one of the losers in a gloomier scenario for the global economy in 2027."
The Australian dollar was trading at US70.20¢ on Tuesday, near its highest level in a month, making it the world's second-best performing currency this year behind Norway's krone.
On the other side of the trade are speculative hedge funds, often dubbed "hot money", which have lifted bets on a strengthening currency, nudging net-long contracts from 50,600 to 52,500 on the CFTC.
Callow said this unusual tension between two cohorts of investors came down to time horizons - hedge funds are hunting for short-term gains, betting the US Federal Reserve will this week keep interest rates on hold while the Reserve Bank will tighten further.
For now, the Australian dollar is trading in the hedge funds' favour. Money markets now imply a 66 per cent chance the RBA will raise the cash rate to 4.85 per cent at its November 3 meeting, up sharply from just a one-in-four shot early this month.
National Australia Bank senior foreign exchange strategist Rodrigo Catril said the market's pivot on rates was a powerful springboard for the currency, with hawkish signals from senior RBA officials keeping buyers engaged ahead of Wednesday's key inflation data.
"The repricing of RBA expectations has been a big factor," Catril said. "We had RBA officials sounding quite hawkish, reminding us all that the RBA is still not yet done in terms of the potential for hiking again."
If this week's inflation report comes in hotter than expected, the central bank could be forced to lift the cash rate for the fifth time this year, triggering a painful currency short squeeze as fund managers are forced to cover their positions. "There's tension from different camps," Catril noted.
Bank of America's Levingston said the hedge fund strategy was a classic yield play during a period of unusually calm currency markets. He added that investors were chasing Australia's higher returns, borrowing in lower-rate currencies like the euro.
Known as a "carry trade", it allows investors to exploit interest rate gaps between nations. Investors borrow cheaply in Europe at a policy rate of 2.5 per cent, and then park the funds in Australia, where the cash rate is 4.6 per cent.
"Hedge funds have been buying the Aussie because it's the high yielder in G10 countries," Levingston said. "As long as FX volatility remains low, the hedge funds will continue to buy."
